body.text: At the high point of the White House state dinner, the hierarchy of the world's two great powers was laid bare.

Around the head table at the centre of the room sat two of the most powerful leaders, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, alongside some of the most influential figures in American technology: Elon Musk, Tim Cook and Taiwanese-born leaders of two of the world's most important chipmakers, Jensen Huang and Lisa Su.
It was an extraordinary encounter between two very different political systems.
On one side was Beijing's political apparatus: Xi's closest diplomats, political architects and economic executors who help consolidate his authority and power.
On the other were the people steering America's capital and technological revolution in AI.
Among Xi's delegation were three of China's most senior political elites: Cai Qi, one of the seven-member Politburo Standing Committee, and Politburo members Wang Yi and He Lifeng.
This was unprecedented and shows Beijing's determination to understand its rival and give the US access to its most powerful political elites.

There was no obvious indication that any of them was being positioned as Xi's successor. But their presence added another layer of political weight to an evening already marked by tensions between the two sides and the quiet shift Xi was projecting to the rest of the world.
The US is no longer at centre of Xi's strategy
Forty years of reform and opening up transformed China into a manufacturing powerhouse and one of the world's largest economies.

When China was keeping a relatively low profile and seeking as many orders from the West as possible for its economic gain, the US had been a dominant force in the international system and central to Beijing's developmental calculations.
That relationship has changed in Xi's era. He has placed greater emphasis on strategic autonomy and technological self-reliance, reducing China's vulnerability to a US-dominated system.
When Xi and Trump both agreed to engage constructively based on respect, fairness and equality, it showed how the relationship has evolved since Xi's first term.
Xi and Trump don't just share the same birth date but also made their political ambitions highly visible.
But Xi has an advantage that Trump as a democratically elected president does not have — time.

For Beijing, a longer political lead time may make it possible to pursue mechanisms that do not lead to an immediate breakthrough but could provide continuity as Trump steps closer to the next election.
By considering each other as equal, both leaders created a strategic framework in which Trump sees Xi as a peer rather than a submissive competitor.

For Xi, as long as the US is clear of Taiwan and South China Sea, mechanisms around AI, trade, fentanyl and Iran's nuclear program could be established to manage the stalemate between the two great powers.
These arrangements, including dialogues, third-party platforms and bilateral boards, could eventually develop into permanent channels, even though strategic competitions will be inevitable.
Xi is taking one step back, so is Trump. It appears to be intentional that larger strategic disagreements and systemic differences remain unresolved.

"The thinking in Beijing may be that while the US remains critical, it need not always be at the centre of China's foreign policy," said Han Lin, Shanghai-based China managing director of American strategic advisory firm The Asia Group.
Xi's projection beyond the bilateral
Since day one of his presidential term in 2013, Xi has increasingly emphasised running the country not solely on Washington's terms.
He has presented China's rise as part of a broader transformation in the global order, expanding Beijing's centralised systems on diplomacy.

Despite two trade wars and national-security accusations from both sides, Xi has sought to manage the fundamental differences between Beijing and Washington to prevent another cold war that could constrain China's growth.

Chinese public's resentment of how the country continuously in building diplomatic capacity is also a factor that Xi knows that Beijing cannot justify its global dominance while millions still live just above the poverty line.
Outside the US-dominated networks, Xi has sought to build coalitions and economic partners across Asia and the Global South, seeking greater influence in institutions that the US does not have a say.

Xi doesn't want China to replace America, he told Trump in Washington again last week. He believes the world can have two great powers on equal terms, allowing both countries to pursue their national interests in different regions.

If this can reduce the risk of a direct conflict between Beijing and Washington, the "constructive strategic stability" relationship, which Xi and Trump agreed to form in Beijing earlier this year, could provide both sides with a framework form managing competition without sparking confrontations.

It could be an attractive solution to the tech giants and policymakers at the White House, where Xi's initiative can appeal to Americans by providing tangible transactions that can manage disagreement.
China's Asia-Pacific ambitions
What Xi wants to realise, on his ultimate political wish list, is a dominant China in Asia and Pacific.
Xi sees it as China's neighbourhood, so he will spare no expense to make sure Washington's strategic presence can be diluted.
Xi's projection of his ambition in Asia Pacific becomes stronger as he walks into new presidential terms — where analysts believe it will happen next year.

His effort in expending China's power alongside his unprecedented authority within the communist party is more obvious through his diplomatic trajectory this year — from the trip to the US, engagement with India through BRICS, and Central Asia for the Shanghai Cooperation Organization.

"It is building coalitions abroad and it's also applying pressure including on America's allies," said Mikko Huotari, executive director of the German-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS).
"China and the US will hold each other in check for the foreseeable future.
"Xi really doesn't need a breakthrough in Washington. He needs more time and the same is true for Washington."
